## Aim

To test whether village boys are more physically fit than town boys using the Mann-Whitney U test in R.

## Practical

The physical fitness measurements of village boys and town boys are given below. Test whether village boys are given below. Test whether village boys are more physically fit than town boys using the Mann-Whitney U test.


It will produce a table like:

| Group | Observations |
|---|---|
| **Village** | 15.7, 8.2, 6.5, 7.2, 9.0, 4.5, 10.6, 12.4, 16.2, 12.9, 11.4, 5.6 |
| **Town** | 12.7, 3.2, 11.8, 7.9, 5.6, 6.7, 12.6, 7.9, 2.7, 6.1, 3.6, 6.5, 2.8 |

## Theory

The **Mann-Whitney U test** is a non-parametric test used to compare two
independent samples. It is an alternative to the independent two-sample
t-test when the assumptions of normality may not be satisfied.

Let

\[
M_V = \text{Median physical fitness measurements of village boys}
\]

and

\[
M_T = \text{Median physical fitness measurements of town boys}.
\]

We are interested in testing whether the median amount for unemployed
students is lower than that for employed students.

### Hypotheses

The null hypothesis is

\[
H_0: M_V = M_T
\]

against the alternative hypothesis

\[
H_1: M_V > M_T
\]

The level of significance is

\[
\alpha = 0.01.
\]

### Test Statistic

All observations from the two groups are combined and ranked from
smallest to largest. If \(R_1\) is the sum of ranks for the unemployed
group and \(R_2\) is the sum of ranks for the employed group, then

\[
U_1 = n_1n_2 + \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2} - R_1
\]


\[
U_2 = n_1n_2 + \frac{n_2(n_2+1)}{2} - R_2
\]

The smaller of the two values is used as the Mann-Whitney U statistic.

The test is one-sided because the alternative hypothesis is

\[
M_V > M_T
\]

## Code

```{r}
# Data

village <- c(15.7, 8.2, 6.5, 7.2, 9.0, 4.5, 10.6, 12.4, 16.2, 12.9, 11.4, 5.6)
town <- c( 12.7, 3.2, 11.8, 7.9, 5.6, 6.7, 12.6, 7.9, 2.7, 6.1, 3.6, 6.5, 2.8)

# Sample sizes

n1 <- length(village)
n2 <- length(town)

cat("Number of village boys:", n1)
cat("Number of town boys:", n2)

# Combine the observations

combined <- c(village, town)

# Calculate ranks

ranks <- rank(combined)

# Sum of ranks for unemployed students

R1 <- sum(ranks[1:n1])

# Sum of ranks for employed students

R2 <- sum(ranks[1:n2])

# Calculate Mann-Whitney U statistic for unemployed group

U1 = (n1*n2) + ((n1*(n1+1))/2) - R1

# Calculate U statistic for employed group

U2 = (n1*n2) + ((n2*(n2+1))/2) - R2

# Smaller U is the Mann-Whitney U statistic

U <- min(U1, U2)

cat("U statistic for unemployed students =", U1, "\n")
cat("U statistic for employed students =", U2, "\n")
cat("Mann-Whitney U statistic =", U, "\n")
```

## Results

Therefore, the calculated Mann-Whitney U statistic is

\[
U_{\text{calculated}}
= 34.
\]

For $n1=12,\ n2=13$ at the 1% level of significance for a one-tailed test, the tabulated critical value is

\[
U_{\text{tabulated}}=27.
\]

Thus,

\[
U_{\text{calculated}}=34
\]

Since

\[
U_{\text{calculated}}>U_{\text{tabulated}},
\]

we **fail to reject \(H_0\)**.

# Conclusion

At the 1% level of significance,

\[
U_{\text{calculated}}=34>U_{\text{tabulated}}=27.
\]

Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Hence, there is not enough evidence to conclude that the village boys are more physically fit than town boys at 1% level of significance.
